title: Lighting appraisal, well-being, and performance in open-plan offices: a linked mechanisms approach
authors: Veitch, J. A.; Newsham, G. R.; Boyce, P. R.; Jones, C. C., 2008
research_question: To test the linked mechanisms by which lighting conditions affect health, well-being, and task performance in open-plan offices.

participants.description: Experiment 1 (between groups, Ex1BG): 151 participants (58 men, 93 women, mean age 34 years). Experiment 1 (repeated measures, Ex1RM): 36 participants (9 men, 27 women, mean age 34 years). Experiment 2 (Ex2): 80 participants (30 men, 50 women, mean age 30.6 years). All were temporary office personnel.
participants.recruitment: Hired from an office temporary services agency.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A simulated open-plan office space with nine cubicles. Six different lighting configurations were used across two experiments, all compliant with existing North American standards for office lighting. These included: 1. Recessed parabolic louvered luminaires (Base Case 1). 2. Suspended linear direct-indirect luminaires (~600 lx desktop illuminance) plus wall washing (Best Practice 1). 3. Best Practice 1 with a switchable desk lamp plus wall washing (Best Practice 1 with switching control). 4. Suspended workstation specific direct-indirect luminaires with individual workstation dimming for the direct portion plus wall washing (Dimming Control). 5. Recessed prismatic lensed luminaires (Base Case 2). 6. Suspended linear direct-indirect luminaires dimmed to 400 lx desktop illuminance plus wall washing (Best Practice 2).

measures.instrument: Persistence at a target identification task (willingness to persist)
Average composite visual performance (correct responses/sec) for a high contrast target
Sum of physical and visual discomfort scores (internal consistency reliability alpha = 0.78-0.86)
Average satisfaction with the work environment
Average satisfaction with one's work performance that day
Time taken between completing parts of summary extraction task (SumBrk)
Speed of response to visual and auditory prompt (ESpd)
Correct characters per second typed in a transcription task (8 pt print)
Average standardized performance speed on three complex tasks (categorizing, judging quality, summarizing)
Average accuracy score for categorizing short articles

findings.antecedent: Individual control over lighting (Dimming Control, Best Practice 1 with switching control)
findings.consequent: Varied luminous conditions (range of light levels chosen)
findings.mechanism: Personal control allows individuals to adjust their environment to meet their needs/preferences.
findings.quote: Personal control resulted in varied luminous conditions. When offered the opportunity to adjust part of the workstation lighting, people chose a wide range of light levels.

findings.consequent: Perceived comfort (rated as comfortable by more people)
findings.mechanism: Direct-indirect lighting provides a more balanced luminance distribution, reducing discomfort.
findings.quote: the lighting from direct-indirect luminaires (Best Practice) was rated as being comfortable by more people (~80%) than that from direct only luminaires (Base Case) (~70%).

findings.antecedent: Individually controllable workstation specific lighting (Dimming Control)
findings.consequent: Perceived comfort (rated as comfortable by more people)
findings.mechanism: Personal control over lighting allows individuals to optimize for their comfort.
findings.quote: Individually controllable workstation specific lighting (Dimming Control) was rated as being comfortable by over 90% of participants.

findings.antecedent: Lighting conditions that improved the visibility of the tasks
findings.mechanism: Improved visibility reduces cognitive load, freeing resources for task performance.
findings.quote: Lighting conditions that improved the visibility of the tasks led to better task performance.

findings.mechanism: Control enhances feelings of competence and autonomy, boosting motivation.
findings.quote: Individual control over lighting beneficially affected motivation and well-being (as measured by satisfaction ratings).

mechanisms: Lighting conditions influence visual capabilities (visibility, comfort) and appraisal (quality, attractiveness).
Appraisal affects preference, which affects mood.
Mood affects health and well-being (discomfort, satisfaction).
Mood and perceived competence affect motivation, which affects task performance.
Personal control over lighting affects mood and feelings of competence.
implementation_implications: Lighting conditions should support high task visibility and favorable appraisals of lighting quality.
Carefully designed direct-indirect lighting systems, especially those with control over the direct component, are most likely to meet these goals.
Individual control over lighting beneficially affects motivation and well-being.
Occupancy sensors, daylight harvesting, and individual control with workstation-specific direct-indirect lighting systems can result in significant energy savings (up to 70%).
Improvements in lighting appraisals from 'good enough' levels lead to improvements in health and well-being, which should benefit organizations.

limitations: The laboratory setting limits generalizability to real offices.
Difficulty in providing sufficiently challenging tasks in a short-term experiment to produce a range of responses in relation to lighting conditions, comfort, or visual capabilities.
The environmental competence scale is relatively new and designed more for field studies than laboratory experiments.
The mediated regression analysis approach cannot give an estimate of the fit of the entire model (unlike structural equation modeling).
Many simultaneous regression analyses increase the possibility of spurious results due to the non-independence of the tests (though addressed by using three separate data sets as replications).
The unexpected negative relationship between preference and motivation needs further research to determine if it is a real phenomenon or a chance occurrence.
Short duration of temporary workers may not adequately show long-term feelings or differences compared to permanent employees.
The findings are indicative for firm recommendations, but longer duration field studies are needed.
The study did not fully explore how lighting in one workstation influenced others in an open-plan setting.

paper_metadata.title: Lighting appraisal, well-being and performance in open-plan offices: A linked mechanisms approach
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Lighting appraisal, well-being and performance in open-plan offices: A linked mechanisms approach
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In two experiments in a simulated office space, temporary office personnel worked under one of six lighting conditions for a day. A previous paper reported the results of statistical tests for lighting conditions effects on perceptions, feelings and task performance. This paper reports mediated regression analyses testing the linked mechanisms by which lighting conditions affect health, well-being and task performance. Combined results from the two statistical approaches show that people who perceived their office lighting as being of higher quality rated the space as more attractive, reported more pleasant mood, and showed greater well-being at the end of the day. Direct—indirect lighting and personal control were favoured. Lighting conditions that improved visibility also improved task performance.
